To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the facial nerve vasomotor system does not increase cortical blood flow in parallel with increases in neuronal activity.

(1) stimulation of the facial vasodilator (VIIIn) nerve increases cerebral blood flow (CBF), (2) this increase is not linked to neuronal activity in the underlying cortex and (3) this lack of linkage is not the result of an alteration in the dynamic flow/metabolisim coupling that normally exists between CBF and neuronal activity.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the parasympatic facial nerve in the regulation of cerebral blood flow and metabolism.
the neural control of cerebral blood flow.
the role of the parasympthetic facial (VII) nerve in the control of cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the VIIn does not appear to increase cerebral blood flow through the same mechanism(s) that is responsible for increases in cerebral metabolism.
VIIn stimulation increases cerebral blood flow in a fashion that is independent of changes in neuronal activity.
cerebral blood flow is coupled to local metabolism but not to neuronal activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the VIIn does not appear to be a significant source of cerebral blood flow regulation.
there is no evidence for a functional link between the facial nerve vasculature and the cortical vasculature.
there is no coupling of cerebral blood flow and neuronal activity during VIIn nerve stimulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the changes in cerebral blood flow that occur with stimulation of VIIn are independent of changes in neuronal activity in the region monitored by the laser Doppler.
the changes in blood flow seen with VIIN stimulation do not occur in parallel with changes seen in neuronal activity.
the VIIn does not appear to be a physiological regulator of cerebral blood flow in the cat.
